title: People and things: 'це', adjectives and possessives
objectives: I can point at people and things with 'це' and ask 'Хто це?', 'Що це?' and 'Яки́й він?'.
I can describe people and things with adjectives that agree with the noun in gender and number, in their hard and soft forms.
I can say whose something is with 'мій', 'твій', 'наш', 'ваш' and 'ї́хній', and with the unchanging 'його́', 'її́' and 'їх'.
I can form the nominative plural of nouns, learning each plural with its stress.
I can name a profession in the form for a man and the form for a woman, and explain how words such as 'вчи́тель', 'дру́зі' and 'си́ній' are spelled and said.

vocabulary.note: Someone who studies at a university or college. The plural 'студе́нти' names men, or a group of men and women together.

example.source: I am a student, and you?

vocabulary.note: Made from 'студе́нт' by adding '-ка'. The plural 'студе́нтки' names women only.
The plural is 'лікарі́': the stress moves to the ending, and the 'р' is soft before 'і'.

example.source: My brother is not a doctor.

vocabulary.note: The everyday word for a woman doctor. The plural is 'лі́карки'.

example.source: She is a doctor, and he is a student.

vocabulary.note: After a consonant and at the start of a sentence it is written 'учи́тель': 'Він учи́тель.' The plural is 'вчителі́', with the stress on the ending.

example.source: Who is this? This is a teacher.

vocabulary.note: The soft sign of 'вчи́тель' stays before '-ка'. After a consonant and at the start of a sentence it is written 'учи́телька'. The plural is 'вчи́тельки'.
The plural is 'дру́зі', with 'з' in place of 'г'. 'Дру́зі' also names a group of friends of both sexes.
Men and women both use it for a woman who is their friend. The plural is 'по́други'.
The stress is on the ending in every form: 'нова́', 'нове́', 'нові́'.
The forms are 'стара́', 'старе́', 'старі́'. Said of a thing it is neutral; said of a person it can sound blunt.
The stress stays on 'ли' in every form: 'вели́ка', 'вели́ке', 'вели́кі'.
The stress is on the ending in every form: 'мала́', 'мале́', 'малі́'.

example.target: Мали́й стіл тут, а вели́кий там.
example.source: The small table is here, and the big one is there.
example.source_literal: small table here, and big there.

vocabulary.note: The forms are 'га́рна', 'га́рне', 'га́рні'. It is used for people, places, things and a fine day.

example.source: It is a nice day today.

vocabulary.note: The forms are 'ціка́ва', 'ціка́ве', 'ціка́ві'. The 'ц' is soft before 'і'.
A soft stem: 'си́ня', 'си́нє', 'си́ні'. It names a deep blue; a light, sky blue is usually the separate word 'блаки́тний'.
It agrees with the thing owned: 'мій', 'моя́', 'моє́', 'мої́'.
For one person you call 'ти': 'твій', 'твоя́', 'твоє́', 'твої́'.
The forms are 'наш', 'на́ша', 'на́ше', 'на́ші'.
For one person you call 'ви', or for several people: 'ваш', 'ва́ша', 'ва́ше', 'ва́ші'.

example.source: Iryna Petrivna, is this your pen?

vocabulary.note: It has the soft endings of 'си́ній': 'ї́хня', 'ї́хнє', 'ї́хні'. The unchanging 'їх' also means 'their'.
It agrees like an adjective: 'яка́', 'яке́', 'які́'. It also opens an exclamation: 'Яка́ га́рна пі́сня!'

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: 'вчи́тель', 'дру́зі', 'си́ній' and the possessives
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit is read with the rules of the earlier units. The words below show those rules at work.

'Вчи́тель' shows three rules. The 'в' stands before a consonant, so it is said [w], as in 'Львів'. The soft sign after 'л' makes the 'л' soft: the middle of the tongue rises toward the palate, close to the 'lli' of 'million'. And the stress can move: in the plural 'вчителі́' it falls on the ending, so learn the plural with its stress, as unit 4 advised for 'рука́' and 'ру́ки'. In 'вчи́телька' the soft sign stays before '-ка', and the 'л' stays soft.

The first sound of 'вчи́тель' follows the euphony rule of unit 4 for 'у' and 'в', the same alternation at the start of a word. After a vowel the word begins with 'в': 'Вона́ вчи́телька.', 'Це вчи́тель.' After a consonant, and at the start of a sentence, it begins with 'у', said [u]: 'Він учи́тель.', 'наш учи́тель'. Both spellings are one word; this course cites it as 'вчи́тель'.

'Дру́зі', the plural of 'друг', applies the alternation of unit 5: before the ending '-і', 'г' becomes 'з', just as 'кни́га' becomes 'у кни́зі'. The 'з' is soft before 'і'. In 'друг' itself the final 'г' stays voiced, the [ɦ] of unit 2.

'Си́ній' has a soft stem: its 'н' is soft in every form. Its endings are written with the letters that soften a consonant (unit 3), '-ій', '-я', '-є' and '-і', where a hard stem has '-ий', '-а', '-е' and '-і'. The 'с' before 'и' stays hard.

The possessives use the letters of unit 3:

- 'Його́' begins with 'йо', the spelling of [jɔ] at the start of a word, and its 'г' is [ɦ].
- 'Її́' is two letters 'ї', each said [ji].
- 'Мої́' and 'твої́' end in 'ї' after a vowel, said [ji].
- 'Моя́' and 'моє́' have 'я' and 'є' after a vowel, said [jɑ] and [jɛ].
- 'Ї́хній' begins with 'ї', said [ji], and its 'н' is soft in every form, as in 'си́ній': 'ї́хня', 'ї́хнє', 'ї́хні'.

rows: 'в' before a consonant is [w]; 'ль' is a soft 'л'
The same word after a consonant, with 'у' by euphony
'л' is soft before 'і'; the stress moves to the ending
A soft 'н' in every form; 'с' is hard before 'и'
'р' is soft before 'і'; the stress moves to the ending
'йо' is [jɔ] at the start of a word; 'г' is [ɦ]

examples.source: He is a teacher, and so is she.

grammar.title: 'Це' and the questions 'Хто це?', 'Що це?' and 'Яки́й?'
grammar.explanation:
'Це' is a demonstrative pronoun, a pronoun that points at something. Put it first and add a noun, and the sentence is complete: 'Це мій брат.' means 'This is my brother', literally 'this my brother'. Ukrainian needs no word for 'is' here (unit 5). 'Це' translates 'this', 'that', 'it', 'these' and 'those', and the situation tells which.

'Це' never changes. English changes 'this is' to 'these are' for more than one, but Ukrainian keeps 'це' and changes only the words after it, which agree with each other:

- 'Це мій брат.' This is my brother.
- 'Це моя́ сестра́.' This is my sister.
- 'Це моє́ вікно́.' This is my window.
- 'Це мої́ дру́зі.' These are my friends.

'Це' introduces someone or something. Once it is introduced, a personal pronoun takes over, chosen by the gender of the noun: 'Це мій брат. Він лі́кар.' means 'This is my brother. He is a doctor.' A name after 'це' stays in the nominative, because no one is being addressed: 'Це Окса́на.' The vocative of unit 7 appears only when you speak to her: 'Окса́но, це Сем.'

Three questions go with 'це':

- 'Хто це?' asks who someone is, literally 'who this?'. Ukrainian also asks 'хто' about animals: 'Хто це? Це мій кіт.'
- 'Що це?' asks what something is, literally 'what this?', and is used for things.
- 'Яки́й?' asks what kind, or what someone or something is like. It is an interrogative pronoun, a pronoun that asks a question, and it agrees like an adjective: 'яки́й' for a masculine noun, 'яка́' for a feminine one, 'яке́' for a neuter one and 'які́' for the plural.

'Яки́й він?' means 'What is he like?', literally 'what-kind he?', and the answer is an adjective: 'Він ціка́вий.' Before a noun in a question, 'яки́й' means 'which' or 'what kind of': 'Яка́ кни́га?' means 'Which book?'. In an exclamation it means 'what a': 'Яка́ ціка́ва кни́га!' is 'What an interesting book!', literally 'what-kind interesting book!'.

A question with no question word is a statement said with a rising voice (unit 5): 'Це твій ключ?' means 'Is this your key?'.

rows: Who is this? This is Olena.
What is this? This is a key.

examples.source: Who is this? This is my cat.
What is this? This is my key.
What is she like? She is interesting.
Oksana, this is my friend Sam.

grammar.title: Adjectives in the nominative: hard and soft stems
grammar.explanation:
An adjective ('прикме́тник', unit 5) describes a noun, and in Ukrainian it agrees with that noun: it takes the noun's gender, number and case. This unit uses the nominative, the case of the subject and of a word that describes the subject. In the nominative an adjective has four forms, one for each gender in the singular and one plural for all three genders. The dictionary form is the masculine.

The endings depend on the adjective's stem, the part before the ending. Most adjectives have a hard stem, which ends in a hard consonant, and take these endings:

- masculine '-ий': 'нови́й стіл', a new table
- feminine '-а': 'нова́ кни́га', a new book
- neuter '-е': 'нове́ вікно́', a new window
- plural '-і': 'нові́ столи́', 'нові́ кни́ги', 'нові́ ві́кна'

A few adjectives have a soft stem, which ends in a soft consonant. Their endings are the same vowel sounds, written with the letters that keep the consonant soft:

- masculine '-ій': 'си́ній оліве́ць', a blue pencil
- feminine '-я': 'си́ня ру́чка', a blue pen
- neuter '-є': 'си́нє о́зеро', a blue lake
- plural '-і': 'си́ні ру́чки', blue pens

The masculine form shows the type: '-ий' marks a hard stem and '-ій' a soft one. Two soft adjectives are already familiar: 'сере́дній' and 'тепе́рішній'.

The gender of the noun decides the form, not the look of its ending. 'День' and 'о́сінь' both end in '-ь', but 'день' is masculine and 'о́сінь' feminine: 'га́рний день', 'га́рна о́сінь'. 'Кафе́' never changes, but it is neuter: 'нове́ кафе́'.

Where the adjective stands changes its job. Before the noun it is part of a phrase: 'нова́ кни́га', 'a new book'. After the noun it is the predicate, the part of a sentence that says something about the subject, and because Ukrainian has no 'is' here, the two words already make a sentence: 'Кни́га нова́.' means 'The book is new', literally 'book new'. In both places the adjective agrees.

The stress of these adjectives stays on the same syllable in all four forms: 'нови́й', 'нова́', 'нове́', 'нові́'; 'ціка́вий', 'ціка́ва', 'ціка́ве', 'ціка́ві'.

grammar.title: Possessives: 'мій', 'твій', 'наш', 'ваш', 'ї́хній', and 'його́', 'її́', 'їх'
grammar.explanation:
A possessive pronoun says whose something is. 'Мій', 'твій', 'наш', 'ваш' and 'ї́хній' agree with the thing owned, exactly as adjectives do: they take its gender and number. The owner does not change the ending. A woman says 'мій брат' and a man says 'моя́ сестра́', because 'брат' is masculine and 'сестра́' is feminine. English 'my' never changes, so this takes practice.

Choose the word by the owner, and its ending by the thing owned:

- 'мій' for 'я': 'мій брат', 'моя́ сестра́', 'моє́ вікно́', 'мої́ дру́зі'
- 'твій' for 'ти', one person you know well: 'твій ключ', 'твоя́ кни́га'
- 'наш' for 'ми': 'наш дім', 'на́ше мі́сто'
- 'ваш' for 'ви', one person you address formally or several people: 'ва́ша ру́чка', 'ва́ші кни́ги'
- 'ї́хній' for 'вони́': 'ї́хній дім', 'ї́хня сім’я́'

The forms of 'мій' and 'твій' write 'я', 'є' and 'ї' after the vowel 'о' ('моя́', 'моє́', 'мої́'). 'Ї́хній' takes the soft endings of 'си́ній'. 'Наш' and 'ваш' have no ending in the masculine and take '-а', '-е' and '-і' in the other forms.

A possessive can also stand without a noun, where English says 'mine', 'yours' or 'ours': 'Кни́га моя́.' means 'The book is mine', literally 'book my'. 'Це твоє́?' means 'Is this yours?'; with no noun named, the possessive takes the neuter form.

'Його́', 'її́' and 'їх' work differently. They are not possessive pronouns but forms of the personal pronouns 'він', 'вона́' and 'вони́' in the genitive, the case that means 'of' (unit 5). 'Його́ сестра́' is literally 'of-him sister'. Because they are forms of another word, they never agree with the thing owned:

- 'його́ брат', 'його́ сестра́', 'його́ дру́зі': his brother, his sister, his friends
- 'її́ брат', 'її́ сестра́', 'її́ дру́зі': her brother, her sister, her friends
- 'їх брат', 'їх сестра́', 'їх дру́зі': their brother, their sister, their friends

Here the choice depends only on the owner, as with English 'his' and 'her'. 'Його́' also means 'its' for a masculine or neuter owner, and 'її́' for a feminine one. 'Their' has two standard forms, the unchanging 'їх' and the agreeing 'ї́хній': 'їх дім' and 'ї́хній дім' both mean 'their house'.

examples.target: Це її́ брат, а це його́ сестра́.
examples.source: This is her brother, and this is his sister.
examples.source_literal: this of-her brother, and this of-him sister.

examples.target: Їх дім стари́й, а ї́хнє кафе́ нове́.
examples.source: Their house is old, and their café is new.
examples.source_literal: of-them house old, and their café new.

grammar.title: The nominative plural of nouns
grammar.explanation:
The nominative plural names more than one person or thing as the subject of a sentence, after 'це', or after a pronoun subject, as in 'Вони́ студе́нти.' Its ending depends on the noun's gender and on whether its stem is hard or soft (unit 3):

- Masculine and feminine nouns with a hard stem take '-и': 'студе́нт', 'студе́нти'; 'кни́га', 'кни́ги'; 'студе́нтка', 'студе́нтки'.
- Masculine and feminine nouns with a soft stem take '-і': 'вчи́тель', 'вчителі́'; 'пі́сня', 'пі́сні'.
- Masculine and feminine nouns whose stem ends in 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' or 'щ' also take '-і': 'ключ', 'ключі́'.
- Neuter nouns take '-а' after a hard stem and '-я' after a soft one: 'вікно́', 'ві́кна'; 'мі́сто', 'міста́'; 'я́блуко', 'я́блука'; 'ре́чення', 'ре́чення'.

The ending replaces the final vowel of the singular, as in 'кни́га' and 'кни́ги', or is added after a final consonant, as in 'студе́нт' and 'студе́нти'. A final soft sign drops, because the ending '-і' now softens the consonant: 'вчи́тель', 'вчителі́'. A neuter noun in '-я' after a doubled consonant, such as 'ре́чення', looks the same in both numbers, and 'кафе́' never changes: 'нові́ кафе́'.

The singular does not always show the plural, so a few nouns are learned with it:

- 'Лі́кар' ends in 'р', which can be hard or soft. In this word it is soft, as the plural shows: 'лікарі́'.
- 'Друг' has a hard stem but takes '-і', and its 'г' becomes 'з' before it: 'дру́зі'.
- 'Стіл' brings back the 'о' of its stem in the open syllable of the plural, as unit 5 explained: 'столи́'.
- 'Украї́нець' and 'кана́дець' lose the 'е' of their last syllable and, with the soft stem 'ць', take '-і': 'украї́нці', 'кана́дці'.

The stress often moves in the plural: 'брат', 'брати́'; 'сестра́', 'се́стри'; 'вчи́тель', 'вчителі́'; 'вікно́', 'ві́кна'; 'мі́сто', 'міста́'. Learn each plural with its stress.

Adjectives and possessives have one plural form for every gender, so 'нові́' and 'мої́' go with any plural noun: 'мої́ нові́ дру́зі', 'мої́ нові́ по́други'. The masculine plural of a noun for people names men, or a group of men and women together: 'студе́нти'. The feminine plural names women only: 'студе́нтки'.

examples.source: My brothers and sisters are here.

grammar.title: Professions: a form for a man and a form for a woman
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian names a profession with a noun, and most professions have two: a masculine noun for a man and a feminine noun for a woman. The feminine is usually made with a suffix, a part added to the end of a word to make a new word. Adding '-ка' turns 'студе́нт' into 'студе́нтка', 'лі́кар' into 'лі́карка', and 'програмі́ст', programmer, into 'програмі́стка'. In 'вчи́телька' the soft sign of 'вчи́тель' stays before the suffix. The nationality words of unit 7 also come in pairs, with '-ка' in place of the masculine '-ець': 'украї́нець', 'украї́нка'. 'По́друга', a woman friend, is built differently and is learned as a word.

To say what someone does, use a pronoun and the profession, with no word for 'is' and no word for 'a': 'Він лі́кар.' means 'He is a doctor', literally 'he doctor'. Choose the form that matches the person: a man says 'Я студе́нт.' and a woman says 'Я студе́нтка.' The form tells the listener whether the speaker is a man or a woman, which English 'I am a student' does not.

As unit 5 explained, written Ukrainian puts a dash between a noun subject and a noun predicate, as in a sentence made of a name and a profession. This course avoids that pattern and uses a pronoun subject ('Вона́ лі́карка.'), 'це' ('Це на́ша лі́карка.') or a negation ('Оле́на не студе́нтка.').

An adjective or a possessive agrees with the form of the profession: 'нови́й учи́тель', 'нова́ вчи́телька'; 'наш лі́кар', 'на́ша лі́карка'. In the plural, 'студе́нти', 'лікарі́' and 'вчителі́' name men or a mixed group, and 'студе́нтки', 'лі́карки' and 'вчи́тельки' name women only.

'Хто він?' and 'Хто вона́?', literally 'who he?' and 'who she?', often ask about someone's profession or role: 'Хто вона́? Вона́ вчи́телька.'

examples.source: He is a doctor, and she is a teacher.
Who is she? She is a programmer.

culture.title: Women's professions, friends and teachers
culture.text:
Ukrainian has long had feminine nouns for women in many professions, and they are the normal way for a woman to name her work: 'Я лі́карка.', 'Я вчи́телька.', 'Я студе́нтка.' The official spelling rules of 2019 describe the suffixes that make such nouns, and newer nouns built the same way, such as 'програмі́стка' (programmer), 'дире́кторка' (director) and 'а́вторка' (author), are now usual in the press, at work and in public life. Some older speakers and some formal documents still use the masculine noun for a woman, but in everyday Ukrainian the feminine form is the expected one.

'Друг' and 'по́друга' are words for real friends, people you are close to, and Ukrainians say 'мій друг' or 'моя́ по́друга' with warmth. A group of friends of both sexes is 'дру́зі', and a group of women friends is 'по́други'. A friend is introduced with the pattern of this unit: 'Це мій друг Тара́с.'

At school and in language courses, students say 'ви' to a teacher and address the teacher by first name and patronymic in the vocative: 'Іри́но Петрі́вно'. Among themselves they speak of 'на́ша вчи́телька' or 'наш учи́тель', with the 'у' that follows a consonant.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English

exercises.explanation: 'Що' asks about a thing and 'це' points at it. Ukrainian needs no word for 'is': literally 'what this?'.

exercises.prompt: Which question does Ukrainian use to ask about an animal, such as a cat?
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian asks 'хто' about people and animals and 'що' about things, so a cat is 'Хто це?'.
'Кни́га' is feminine and singular, so the adjective takes the feminine ending '-а': 'нова́ кни́га'.
'Кіт' is masculine, so the possessive takes its masculine form, 'мій'.
A woman takes the feminine form 'вчи́телька'. After the vowel that ends 'вона́', the word begins with 'в'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence can only be said by a woman?
exercises.explanation: 'Студе́нтка' is the feminine form of the profession, so the speaker is a woman. 'Тут' never changes, and 'моя́' agrees with 'кни́га', not with the speaker.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'це' stay the same in 'Це мій брат' and 'Це мої́ дру́зі'?
choices: 'Це' never changes; the possessive and the noun after it agree with each other
exercises.explanation: 'Це' points and is invariable. English changes 'this is' to 'these are'; Ukrainian changes only 'мій' to 'мої́', to agree with the plural 'дру́зі'.
'О́зеро' is neuter. 'Си́ній' has a soft stem, so its neuter ending is '-є', where a hard stem has '-е'.

exercises.hint_source: Yes, it is interesting, but old.
exercises.explanation: 'Вона́' stands for 'кни́га', a feminine noun, so 'стари́й' takes its feminine form 'стара́'.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase or sentence with its meaning
Taras asks 'Яка́ вона́?' about Olena's new friend. What does he want to know?
exercises.explanation: 'Яка́' is the feminine of 'яки́й', which asks what kind. About a person it asks what she is like, and the answer is an adjective: 'Вона́ ціка́ва.'

exercises.prompt: Which word means 'her', as in 'her brother'?
exercises.explanation: 'Її́' is the genitive of 'вона́', literally 'of her'. 'Його́' means 'his', and 'їх' and 'ї́хній' both mean 'their'.
'His' is 'його́', the genitive of 'він'. It never changes, so it is the same before 'сестра́' as before 'брат'.

exercises.prompt: Why do we say both 'його́ брат' and 'його́ сестра́', with the same 'його́'?
choices: Possessive pronouns agree only in the plural
'Його́' is used only before words for family
'Його́' is a form of 'він' meaning 'of him', so it does not agree with the thing owned
exercises.explanation: 'Його́' is the genitive of 'він', not a possessive pronoun. Only the owner decides it, as with English 'his'; 'мій', 'твій', 'наш', 'ваш' and 'ї́хній' are the words that agree.

exercises.prompt: At the new café, Bohdan says 'Воно́ мале́, але́ моє́.' Why 'моє́'?
choices: It is the form a man uses
It agrees with 'кафе́', which is neuter
exercises.explanation: A possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. 'Кафе́' is neuter, so 'мій' takes its neuter form 'моє́', here meaning 'mine'.
The plural of 'друг' takes '-і', and before it 'г' becomes 'з', as in 'у кни́зі': 'дру́зі'. If all the friends are women, 'по́други' is also correct.

exercises.prompt: Which adjective has a soft stem?
exercises.explanation: The masculine ending shows the type: '-ій' marks a soft stem, so 'си́ній' has the forms 'си́ня', 'си́нє', 'си́ні'. The others end in '-ий' and have hard stems.

exercises.hint_source: Are these your keys? (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: A friend is someone you call 'ти', so 'your' is 'твій', and with the plural 'ключі́' it takes the plural form 'твої́'.

exercises.prompt: In which pair does the stress move to the ending in the plural?
exercises.explanation: 'Брат' has one syllable, and in the plural 'брати́' the stress falls on the ending. In the other pairs it stays on the stem. Learn each plural with its stress.
'Вчи́тель' has a soft stem, so its plural takes '-і', the soft sign drops and the stress moves: 'вчителі́'. If all the teachers are women, 'вчи́тельки' is also correct.

exercises.prompt: Oksana says 'Вони́ вчителі́' about her mom and dad. Why 'вчителі́' and not 'вчи́тельки'?
choices: The masculine plural names a group of men and women together
exercises.explanation: 'Вчи́тельки' names women only. Her dad is a man, so the mixed group takes the masculine plural 'вчителі́'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'Він учи́тель' but 'Вона́ вчи́телька'?
choices: The word begins with the 'у' or 'в' of the euphony rule: 'у' after a consonant, 'в' after a vowel
'У' marks the form for a man and 'в' the form for a woman
exercises.explanation: 'Він' ends in a consonant, so the word begins with 'у'; 'вона́' ends in a vowel, so it begins with 'в'. The same rule chooses between the prepositions 'у' and 'в'.
'Це' and a noun make the sentence, with no word for 'is'. 'Моя́' agrees with the feminine 'вчи́телька', which begins with 'в' after the vowel of 'моя́'.
'Кафе́' never changes its form, but it is neuter, so 'на́ше' and 'мале́' take neuter endings. No word for 'is' is needed.

exercises.prompt_source: They are not teachers, they are doctors.

exercises.explanation: 'Студе́нти' names men or a mixed group, and 'студе́нтки' women only. A pronoun subject and the plural noun make the sentence.

exercises.prompt_source: His sister is not a student.
exercises.explanation: 'Його́' never changes, 'не' goes before the word it negates, and the profession takes the feminine form 'студе́нтка' to match the sister.
